Stagnant Housing Market? Not for Luxury Homes
 
And, real-estate giant CBRE is acquiring a company that equips data centers in a $1 billion deal
 
By Craig Karmin
 

This is an edition of the Real Estate newsletter, a weekly briefing of the biggest commercial deals, news, analysis and trends in office, multifamily, retail and other commercial sectors. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 

The U.S. housing market is splintering. On one side, near-record home prices and the recent surge in mortgage rates have pushed many buyers to the sidelines. Sales are stagnant and sellers are cutting prices. On the other side is a robust luxury market where wealthier home shoppers can steer clear of high rates with jumbo down payments or all-cash purchases. As Nicholas G. Miller reports, the top third of the market is spending enough that it’s pushed up home prices nationally by more than 4% over the past two years.

 

Peter Grant has an AI scoop: Real estate giant CBRE is acquiring a company that equips data centers in a $1 billion deal. It’s the latest sign that commercial real estate is tying its growth to the AI spending boom. The world’s largest commercial real estate services firm is expanding from bricks and mortar services in data centers to installing the cabling and connections that enable servers to power artificial intelligence. The recent purchases take CBRE into “where the actual compute happens,” said CBRE Chief Executive Bob Sulentic.

 
 
 

America’s New Housing Market Is All About Luxury—and It Runs on Cash

 
 
DAVID PAUL MORRIS/BLOOMBERG NEWS
 

America’s home-buying market is a house divided. In many cities, sales are stagnant and sellers are cutting prices for lower-end and entry-level homes to lure back buyers.

 

The top third of the market is still buying, and spending enough to push up home prices nationally by more than 4% over the past two years.

 
 
 

Real-Estate Giant CBRE Gets Deeper Into Data Centers With $1 Billion Deal

 
 
CBRE
 

Real-estate giant CBRE is acquiring a company that equips data centers in a $1 billion deal, the latest sign that commercial-real estate is tying its growth to the AI spending boom.

 
 
 
1.4%
 

The vacancy rate for data-center real estate in the year that ended June 30, according to CBRE. Data-center capacity grew nearly 34% over the same period in eight major U.S. markets as the technology sector continues to fuel commercial-real-estate growth.

 
 
 

The Holdouts Working Around New York City’s Airbnb Crackdown

 
 
MIKEY GULCICEK FOR THE WALL STREET JOURNAL
 

New York City three years ago enacted one of the country’s strictest crackdowns on short-term rentals, which reduced the number of listings across the five boroughs by more than 90%. The Wall Street Journal spoke with several New York City homeowners who continue to host Airbnb guests about their experiences.

 
 
 

Data Points

 

• 1.5 million: The amount, in square feet, of New York City office real estate leased by AI companies through the first nine months of this year, according to CoStar. That is more than twice the total amount leased in all of 2025 as companies in the fast-growing sector expand their footprints to accommodate increased head count.

 

• 10 million: The amount, in square feet, of retail-real estate projects developers broke ground on in the third quarter, the lowest quarterly total for retail-construction starts since at least 2007, according to CoStar. Despite strong demand by retailers for new store space, increased construction and borrowing costs have hampered new developments.

 

• 7.3% The month-over-month decline in pending home sales in September, the lowest level since at least 2001, according to the National Association of Realtors’ pending home sales index. Mortgage rates, now above 7%, are eroding buying power even during the fall season, which typically favors buyers.
